newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kinkel criticises Turkish leaders over fire accusations.
newsitem.headline: Kinkel criticises Turkish leaders over fire accusations.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel criticised Turkish political leaders on Saturday for anti-German remarks made after an arson attack that killed three Turks in Krefeld, Germany last Monday.
"Unacceptable comments from the Turkish side are not needed," Kinkel said according to an advance text of the Sunday newspaper Welt am Sonntag.

Kinkel said Turkish leaders should refrain from making hasty accusations after police determined the fatal fire that Turkish prime minister, Necmettin Erbakan, had blamed on rising anti-Moslem sentiment in the West was started by a Turkish man.

"This sort of megaphone-diplomacy leads nowhere. It only destroys ties that have been built up over a long period of time," Kinkel told the Welt am Sonntag newspaper, referring to Erbakan's comments as well as remarks by Turkey's Interior Minister Meral Aksener.
Aksener was quoted by the semi-official Anatolian news agency as saying on Thursday that "they (Germans) couldn't throw us out, now they are trying to burn us out".

Police, who had said during their investigation there was no evidence of a racist attack, announced on Friday they believed the fire in which a woman and her two children perished was deliberately set by her husband, whom she planned to divorce.
The German government summoned Turkey's ambassador to protest at the criticism from Ankara.
"Germany and Turkey are important partners for each other," Kinkel said. "Turks living in Germany are welcome and can count on the state to protect them," he added.
The unusually strong language from Germany's top diplomat came as Focus news magazine reported the Bonn government was considering withdrawing an invitation to Erbakan to visit Germany in the autumn.
The magazine quoted government sources in Bonn saying that "without an adequate signal of regret" from Erbakan, it would be "unimaginable" that Kohl would see Erbakan.
Police in the town of Krefeld said the dead woman's 42-year-old husband was remanded in custody on suspicion of starting the fire.
Walter Seifert, the head of Krefeld's murder squad, said an eyewitness had seen the suspect filling a canister with petrol at a filling station.

Seifert said investigations indicated that the suspect had regularly beaten his wife and children and brought a prostitute to live in the apartment for a time. He said the wife had planned to sue for divorce in the next few days.

The wife was fatally injured when she jumped from their third-floor in the town centre. A 16-year-old daughter died in hospital from injuries and a 17-year-old son was found dead in the building. Two other daughters also jumped from the flat and were severely injured.

Erbakan's comments had fuelled a war of words between Turkey and Germany, which is particularly sensitive to such accusations that it is soft on racism after working hard to quell an upsurge of anti-foreigner attacks after unification in 1990.
More than 30 people died then, among them five Turkish women and children in a single attack in Solingen in 1993.

Cornelia Schmalz-Jacobsen, the German government's ombudsman for foreign affairs, warned that the "totally exaggerated" reaction in Turkey to the fire could have a negative impact on German-Turk relations in Germany.
